entries.title: Despite community opposition to data centers, lawmakers offer no clear plan for addressing local concerns
entries.summary: As pushback to data center projects has grown, lawmakers offer no clear plans to address concerns. Others have dismissed community worries altogether.
entries.content:
In April, after residents in Tucker County learned of a bill that could strip their say over a data center project proposed in their backyard, the community mobilized to oppose the project and legislation.

But it was too late.

The bill had passed and the community’s petition to Gov. Patrick Morrisey to veto the measure fell on deaf ears. The governor signed the bill into law despite the public outrage. It removed communities’ authority to restrict noise, lighting and land use from such projects. It also diverted most of the tax revenue from the projects to the state.

Now, as proposals for data center projects begin to pop up across West Virginia, calls on state leaders to amend the legislation to address their concerns about lack of transparency and local control have intensified.

And despite the opposition, the Republican leaders in the Legislature and the governor’s office had no clear plan or outright dismissed calls to roll back the sweeping law benefiting developers.

“For the state government to say you don’t matter, and you don’t get to decide what happens in your community like that’s a slap in the face,” Dylan Jones, a Tucker County resident, said of the legislation.

“That’s just really upsetting. And I think it says a lot about the current administration and how they view the citizens and what their priorities are,” he added.

During a November public meeting, a Tucker County resident asked Sen. Randy Smith, R-Preston, the president of the West Virginia Senate, what he would like to see changed in the state’s data center policy.

Smith said he wants to see more local control restored and more distance between projects and populated areas.

“Everybody wants one, but not in the backyard,” Smith said, in audio from the meeting recorded by Country Roads News, a newsletter dedicated to Tucker County.

But Smith has not outlined any specific bills that he — as one of the most powerful politicians at the Statehouse — would introduce when lawmakers return for the 2026 legislative session.

Speaker of the House Roger Hanshaw, R-Clay, who leads the House of Delegates, didn’t take a position and noted that the legislation was only a few months old.

“One of the things that we always have to do as a legislature is learn from what we’ve done,” Hanshaw said during a December press conference. “I’m sure that it’s among the things we’ll talk about when we convene next month.”

Morrisey said he doesn’t believe the issues with the state’s data center law, which have sparked protests, contentious public meetings and legal challenges, are warranted. Instead, he touted how proceeds from data center development would go toward cutting the personal income tax.

“I would ask the people to take a look at what we’re going to do and judge us by our actions, not by a couple people, a minority, engaging in scare tactics,” Morrisey said during a December press conference in Charleston.

Delegates in areas where the data center projects have been proposed have mixed views.

Del. John Paul Hott, R-Grant, said he is open to tweaking the law to allow for more local control and has been in contact with Smith about doing that.

Both men represent Tucker County, which has the highest profile of these projects. A company has proposed building an off-grid power plant between the towns of Thomas and Davis to power a large data center complex.

Hott noted that eliminating local control was intended to streamline data center development.

“It’s an interesting dilemma, because I’ve always said that I want to be about local control, that always seems to be appropriate, to allow those who are living there and working there to have input,” Hott said.

Yet, when two House Democrats tried to amend more local control into the 2025 bill, Republicans voted it down. On the floor, Del. Clay Riley, R-Harrison, said data center projects carry too much promise for the state’s economic well-being to be held up by the people living next to these projects.

Del. Evan Hansen, D-Monongalia, was one of the Democrats who proposed that amendment in the last session. In the 2026 session, Hansen said he will introduce two pieces of legislation: one to restore local control and another to make developers publicly disclose how water will be used in these projects prior to getting approval.

“I think that there might be some openness among legislators of both parties to address those issues,” Hansen said.

But Democrats, who only have 11 members out of 134 between the House and the Senate, have little political power in Charleston. It’s up to the Republicans to decide how to proceed.

Some Republicans have chosen silence, like Del. Mark Dean, of Mingo County, where a project is being challenged by locals. He didn’t respond to multiple attempts to be interviewed.

Over in Mason County, both Republican Dels. Jim Butler and Jonathan Pinson understand the concerns over the project proposed for their community, but have differing perspectives on amending the governor’s bill.

Pinson said he’s open to addressing issues with local participation, but also noted that this legislation made the state competitive in a way it wasn’t before.

“Being able to make West Virginia competitive was a huge step. Now, are there ways to go back and consider improvements and changes? Absolutely. I’m certain of that,” Pinson said.

Butler also said he would consider amending the current law, but only if there is a “legitimate concern.”

So far though, Butler said there hasn’t been anything he believes needs to be changed.

“You’re always going to have somebody who says, ‘Well, I’ve lived here 30 years. I don’t want to move and I don’t want this place in my backyard,’” Butler said. “But sometimes you just have to do things for the betterment of the whole community.”
entries.author: Henry Culvyhouse, Sarah Elbeshbishi
